items.prompt: A workload stores independent documents accessed by key, with no need for a mounted filesystem or block device. Which storage model fits?
constraints: The application can use an API.

options.text: Use object storage such as Amazon S3, choosing performance features from request rate, object size, and access pattern.
Use a single EBS volume mounted by every Region.
Use EFS because every object workload requires POSIX files.
Use a block device for each document and manage device mappings in the application.

feedback.Reason: Independent key-addressed documents fit object storage rather than a shared filesystem or per-document block device.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: S3 provides scalable object access through APIs and does not require a mounted file or block interface.
Details.scenarioApplication: The application uses object keys and metadata and measures request and object-size behavior for performance.
Details.errorCorrection: EBS is a block volume, EFS is a filesystem, and per-document block devices create unnecessary management.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Object semantics differ from filesystem and block semantics, so applications must handle keys, metadata, and consistency expectations.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: EBS is not a cross-Region shared object API.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A POSIX filesystem is unnecessary for independently addressed objects.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Per-document block devices add operational overhead and do not provide the object model.

items.prompt: A transactional database needs low-latency random reads and writes from an EC2 instance. Which storage interface is the natural starting point?
constraints: The database expects a block device.
The volume is attached to compute.

options.text: Use an appropriately sized EBS volume and select its type from the database's IOPS, throughput, latency, and durability requirements.
Store each database page as a separate S3 object and emulate a block device in the application.
Use CloudFront as the database block layer.
Use an S3 website endpoint for synchronous database writes.

feedback.Reason: EBS presents persistent block storage for EC2 and lets the architect choose IOPS and throughput characteristics.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Database engines use block semantics, while EBS volume type and size determine relevant performance capabilities.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner measures random I/O, queueing, throughput, and growth and then selects and validates an EBS configuration.
Details.errorCorrection: S3 and CloudFront are not block devices or synchronous database storage interfaces.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Higher performance volume choices cost more and may still be bounded by instance EBS bandwidth.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Object APIs do not provide a database block device without changing semantics and latency.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: CloudFront is a delivery cache, not persistent block storage.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: An S3 website endpoint is not a database write path.

items.prompt: Several Linux instances in different Availability Zones need concurrent access to the same POSIX directory tree. Which service fits the access model?

options.text: Use a Regional EFS file system with mount targets and security controls appropriate for the clients and throughput needs.
Attach one EBS volume to all instances simultaneously without a supported clustered filesystem.
Use S3 and assume applications can use POSIX locks directly.
Copy a local directory to each instance and ignore synchronization.

feedback.Reason: EFS provides shared file-system semantics for multiple clients across AZs.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: EFS exposes a managed NFS file system with mount targets and throughput modes for shared access.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect mounts the file system from each AZ, controls network access, and sizes throughput from concurrent workload behavior.
Details.errorCorrection: A single EBS attachment is not the general shared filesystem pattern, S3 has object semantics, and local copies diverge.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: EFS performance and cost depend on throughput and access mode, so workload measurement remains required.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: One EBS volume does not provide safe concurrent filesystem access to arbitrary instances.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: S3 does not provide POSIX locking and mounted filesystem semantics by default.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Independent local copies do not guarantee shared state.

items.prompt: A media pipeline reads and writes large files sequentially and is limited by sustained throughput rather than random IOPS. What signal should dominate storage selection?
constraints: Large files are processed in batches.

options.text: Measure sustained MiB/s, queueing, concurrency, and end-to-end processing time, then choose a storage configuration that meets throughput without overbuying IOPS.
Select the highest IOPS volume regardless of throughput or workload shape.
Use object count as the only performance signal.
Choose the smallest volume because sequential access is always fast.

feedback.Reason: Sequential workloads are commonly constrained by sustained throughput and pipeline concurrency rather than random IOPS alone.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Storage and instance limits expose separate IOPS and throughput dimensions that must be matched to workload behavior.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team benchmarks file size, parallelism, throughput, and processing latency before choosing a volume or file service.
Details.errorCorrection: Maximum IOPS may not improve sequential throughput, object count is indirect, and small capacity can constrain performance.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Higher throughput settings cost more and can move the bottleneck to network or compute.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Random IOPS capability does not automatically solve a sequential throughput bottleneck.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Count does not measure bytes per second or queueing.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Capacity and performance limits are separate and must both be checked.

items.prompt: An analytics service needs durable objects, metadata, parallel retrieval, and independent scaling of storage from compute. Which model is appropriate?
constraints: Objects are immutable after write in the workflow.

options.text: Use S3 object storage with an intentional key layout, metadata strategy, parallel access, and lifecycle or replication controls as needed.
Use one EBS volume attached to a single analytics instance forever.
Use EFS for every object and require all consumers to mount it.
Store objects in instance memory and recreate them after failure.

feedback.Reason: S3 decouples durable object storage from compute and supports metadata and parallel API access.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: S3 objects are addressed by key and can be consumed by many clients without a shared block attachment.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner designs prefixes, metadata, request concurrency, and data protection from the analytics access pattern.
Details.errorCorrection: A single EBS attachment couples storage to one instance, EFS adds unnecessary filesystem semantics, and memory is not durable.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Object workflows need explicit partitioning, consistency, and format decisions rather than filesystem assumptions.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: The single instance is a scaling and failure dependency.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A shared filesystem is not required for independent objects.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Instance memory is lost on failure and restart.

items.prompt: A legacy application requires shared file locks and directory rename semantics across several Linux hosts. Which signal drives the storage choice?
constraints: Multiple hosts access the same namespace.

options.text: Choose a shared file service that supports the required client and locking semantics, then test application behavior and throughput under concurrency.
Move files to S3 without changing the application because object keys equal paths.
Use independent EBS volumes and synchronize directories by timestamp.
Use instance store because it provides the fastest shared locks.

feedback.Reason: File locking and namespace semantics are access-pattern requirements that object and local storage do not automatically provide.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A shared filesystem exposes directory and file operations to multiple clients; performance mode and locking behavior must match the application.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team validates EFS or an appropriate FSx service with the actual legacy workload and failure behavior.
Details.errorCorrection: S3 requires an application change, timestamp sync can lose concurrent updates, and instance store is local and ephemeral.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Managed filesystem throughput, protocol, and lock semantics need compatibility testing and capacity planning.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Object storage does not implement the required POSIX operations automatically.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Timestamp synchronization is not a safe shared lock protocol.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Instance store is local to an instance and not durable shared storage.

items.prompt: A workload needs a block device for an EC2 database and fast environment cloning for tests. Which capability is useful?

options.text: Use EBS snapshots or an equivalent volume-copy workflow, then validate restore time, initialization behavior, and application consistency.
Copy mounted block files with a shell command while the database writes freely.
Use S3 lifecycle rules as a block snapshot mechanism.
Recreate the database from memory after each test.

feedback.Reason: EBS snapshots provide a managed copy mechanism for volumes, but application consistency and restore performance still need validation.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Snapshots capture EBS volume state and can create new volumes for recovery or test environments.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team coordinates database flush or backup semantics, restores a test volume, and measures initialization and query performance.
Details.errorCorrection: Live file copying may be inconsistent, S3 lifecycle is not a block snapshot, and memory is not durable.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Snapshot restore and volume initialization can affect time-to-ready and should be included in RTO testing.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: File-level copy during writes may not be application-consistent.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Lifecycle rules manage objects, not EBS block state.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Memory cannot recreate durable database state reliably.

items.prompt: A shared file workload slows as many clients read and write concurrently. What evidence should guide tuning?
constraints: Throughput and metadata operations both matter.

options.text: Measure throughput, I/O size, metadata rate, client concurrency, burst behavior, and queueing, then choose the file-system performance mode and client layout from the evidence.
Increase file names' length because metadata operations become faster.
Move all files to one directory to simplify access.
Use CPU average as the only storage metric.

feedback.Reason: File performance depends on workload shape and concurrency, not one generic resource metric.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: File throughput and metadata behavior vary with I/O size, client count, namespace operations, and selected performance mode.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner benchmarks the real access pattern, distributes clients appropriately, and validates the selected mode under peak load.
Details.errorCorrection: Long names do not generally solve a metadata bottleneck, one directory can create contention, and CPU is indirect.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Higher file throughput modes and client changes can add cost or migration work.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Name length is not a general control for file-system throughput.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A single namespace hotspot can worsen metadata contention.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: CPU does not identify filesystem queueing or metadata pressure.

items.prompt: Before choosing among object, file, and block storage, which workload profile is most important?
constraints: Performance requirements are not yet quantified.
The application has known access operations.

options.text: Document interface semantics, access pattern, latency, IOPS, throughput, concurrency, sharing, durability, growth, and failure behavior before selecting a service.
Choose the service with the highest advertised capacity.
Choose based only on the file extension of the data.
Use the cheapest storage before measuring workload behavior.

feedback.Reason: Storage selection is driven by access semantics and measured performance, not capacity or price alone.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Object, file, and block services expose different APIs, sharing, latency, scaling, durability, and operational boundaries.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect maps workload signals to a service and validates the selected configuration with representative benchmarks.
Details.errorCorrection: Maximum capacity does not imply correct semantics, file extensions are irrelevant, and lowest price can violate performance or reliability.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A broader profile requires analysis effort but avoids replatforming caused by an incorrect interface choice.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Capacity alone does not establish interface or performance fit.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: File format does not determine storage access semantics.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Cost without workload evidence can create failure or rework.

items.prompt: An S3 client processes large independent objects slowly because it uses one serial request worker. What should be evaluated?
constraints: The network and service can support more concurrency.

options.text: Use bounded parallel requests with appropriate multipart or range behavior, measure throughput and throttling, and keep retries safe and controlled.
Open unbounded concurrency until every request fails.
Store all objects in one EBS volume to force sequential throughput.
Disable retries so a single failure stops the whole transfer.

feedback.Reason: Independent object operations can often use bounded parallelism to improve throughput while respecting client and service limits.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: S3 performance depends on request concurrency, object size, transfer strategy, and retry behavior.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team benchmarks worker count, uses multipart for large objects where appropriate, and bounds retries and bandwidth.
Details.errorCorrection: Unbounded concurrency causes throttling, EBS changes the interface, and disabling retries loses recoverable work.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: More concurrency consumes network and client resources and requires backpressure.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Unbounded requests can overload clients and trigger throttling.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Moving to block storage changes the workload model and adds coupling.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Safe transient failures need a bounded retry path.

items.prompt: An EBS volume has sufficient provisioned IOPS, but application throughput remains below target. What boundary should be checked?
constraints: The volume is attached to EC2.
The instance has finite EBS bandwidth.

options.text: Measure the EC2 instance's EBS bandwidth and queueing as well as volume limits, then size both instance and volume for the workload.
Increase volume IOPS indefinitely without checking the instance.
Move the volume to S3 without changing the application.
Disable monitoring because IOPS is already provisioned.

feedback.Reason: EBS performance is bounded by both volume capabilities and the attached instance's EBS bandwidth.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Provisioned volume IOPS or throughput cannot exceed the path available through the EC2 instance and workload queueing.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect correlates volume and instance metrics and chooses a compatible pair after testing.
Details.errorCorrection: More volume IOPS cannot bypass an instance boundary, S3 changes semantics, and monitoring is needed to find the bottleneck.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A larger instance may cost more and alter compute capacity, so the design should size the complete path.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: The attached instance can remain the limiting path.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: S3 is not a transparent block replacement for a database or filesystem.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Without metrics the bottleneck cannot be confirmed.

items.prompt: A Windows application requires SMB shares, Windows ACLs, and high-throughput shared file access. Which storage signal is decisive?

options.text: Evaluate an FSx for Windows File Server design, including SMB, Active Directory integration, throughput, availability, and client access patterns.
Use S3 because Windows ACLs are identical to object tags.
Use EBS attached to one Windows instance and expose it through an unsupported share.
Use instance store to gain durable shared files.

feedback.Reason: Windows SMB and ACL semantics point to a compatible managed file service rather than object or local block storage.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: FSx for Windows File Server provides managed SMB file shares and integrates with Windows-oriented identity and access patterns.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect validates directory integration, throughput, failover, permissions, and application behavior under concurrency.
Details.errorCorrection: S3 object tags do not provide Windows share semantics, one EBS host is a failure boundary, and instance store is ephemeral.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: FSx configuration and throughput cost must be sized from the workload and availability requirement.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Object tags are not SMB shares or Windows ACL behavior.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A single host creates a bottleneck and unsupported sharing path.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Instance store does not provide durable shared files.

items.prompt: A shared volume is proposed as a single point for two application tiers in different failure domains. What should the architect question?
constraints: A storage failure can affect both.
The access model is not yet justified.

options.text: Check whether shared storage is required, identify its failure and throughput boundary, and separate or replicate data when the shared volume would couple independent tiers.
Share the volume because fewer resources always improve availability.
Put both tiers on one instance to avoid network storage.
Use a larger volume without analyzing failure scope.

feedback.Reason: A shared storage path can create coupling and a common failure boundary between otherwise independent components.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Storage architecture affects failure isolation, scaling, network path, consistency, and access semantics.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect retains shared storage only where the workload requires it and designs availability and performance around the dependency.
Details.errorCorrection: Fewer resources do not automatically improve availability, one instance is a larger SPOF, and volume size does not remove shared failure.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Replicating or separating data adds complexity and may change application semantics.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A shared resource can reduce fault isolation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: One instance increases compute and storage coupling.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Size does not define or remove the failure domain.

items.prompt: A dataset grows unpredictably and storage latency degrades near capacity. Which planning evidence is needed?
constraints: The application has a latency SLO.

options.text: Measure growth rate, usable capacity, performance near capacity, expansion lead time, and failure behavior, then automate alerts and capacity actions.
Wait until storage is full because capacity can be added instantly in every service.
Delete old data without a retention decision.
Use the largest possible storage volume without monitoring.

feedback.Reason: Capacity planning must account for growth, performance, expansion time, retention, and the service's actual limits.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Storage capacity and performance headroom are operational signals, and expansion behavior differs by service and volume type.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team alarms before the safe threshold, sizes expansion, and preserves data according to an approved retention policy.
Details.errorCorrection: Waiting for full capacity is late, deletion without governance risks data, and maximum size without monitoring is not a plan.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: More headroom costs money and may require migration or expansion testing.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Capacity and performance failures can occur before an exact full state.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Retention and deletion must be business and compliance decisions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Large capacity does not eliminate growth or performance monitoring.

items.prompt: A legacy file application is being redesigned to process independent immutable media objects. Which change can improve scaling?
constraints: Objects can be addressed by key.
POSIX locking is no longer required.

options.text: Move the data model toward S3 objects and decouple consumers from a shared filesystem, after validating key, metadata, concurrency, and consistency behavior.
Keep a single shared directory because object access cannot scale.
Put every object on a separate EBS volume.
Use local instance storage as the durable source of truth.

feedback.Reason: When file semantics are no longer required, object storage can decouple storage from compute and scale access by key.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: S3 provides durable, independently scalable object access and metadata rather than one shared namespace.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team updates producers and consumers, preserves required metadata and idempotency, and benchmarks parallel object operations.
Details.errorCorrection: A single directory can become a shared dependency, per-object volumes are unmanageable, and local storage is not durable.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The redesign changes API and consistency semantics and must not be applied to workloads that still require POSIX behavior.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A shared filesystem can preserve unnecessary coupling when file semantics are not needed.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Per-object block volumes add excessive management and attachment constraints.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Instance storage is ephemeral and not a durable source of truth.

items.prompt: A database team creates an EBS snapshot while the database is processing writes and later sees recovery errors. What should improve?
constraints: The database has application consistency requirements.
The team can coordinate a backup window.

options.text: Use a database-consistent backup or coordinated quiesce and validate restore behavior rather than relying only on crash-consistent volume state.
Take more snapshots at the same uncontrolled moment.
Increase the EBS volume size to make the snapshot logically consistent.
Delete the database logs before taking the snapshot.

feedback.Reason: A storage snapshot can be durable yet not represent a database-consistent recovery point without coordination.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Application consistency requires flush, quiesce, database backup semantics, or log-based recovery appropriate to the engine.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner coordinates the snapshot or backup and tests startup, integrity, and transaction recovery from it.
Details.errorCorrection: More uncontrolled copies repeat the inconsistency, size does not change semantics, and deleting logs removes recovery information.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Quiescing writes can affect availability, so the design may use online database backup or replicas.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: More snapshots taken at an unsafe point do not improve consistency.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Volume capacity does not define database consistency.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Logs may be required to recover committed transactions and should not be deleted.

items.prompt: A file application is slow, but CPU and network utilization look low. Which investigation is most useful?
constraints: The storage path has multiple layers.

options.text: Correlate application latency with storage queueing, I/O size, metadata operations, client waits, and service metrics to isolate the constrained layer.
Scale compute immediately without measuring storage behavior.
Assume low CPU proves the file service is healthy.
Delete old files until latency improves without checking the cause.

feedback.Reason: Storage bottlenecks can appear as queueing or metadata waits while compute and network averages remain low.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Performance diagnosis needs end-to-end latency and layer-specific signals such as queue depth, I/O size, metadata rate, and client wait.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team identifies the constrained layer before choosing a volume, file mode, client change, or data layout correction.
Details.errorCorrection: Blind compute scaling may not affect storage, low CPU is indirect, and deletion can be destructive and unrelated.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Fine-grained telemetry costs effort but avoids expensive changes that do not address the bottleneck.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Compute may not be the constrained layer.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Low CPU does not rule out storage wait.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Deletion without diagnosis can lose data and leave latency unchanged.

items.prompt: A team proposes moving a block-backed application to object storage solely because object storage scales more easily. What must be challenged?
constraints: The application currently uses block operations.
The proposal changes the storage interface.

options.text: Confirm whether the application can adopt object semantics, then evaluate API, consistency, concurrency, latency, data layout, and migration changes before selecting S3.
Move immediately because higher scalability always improves the workload.
Keep both interfaces writing the same data without reconciliation.
Use object storage as a transparent block device without an adapter or redesign.

feedback.Reason: Changing storage interface changes application semantics and must be justified by workload fit, not scalability in isolation.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Block, file, and object models differ in addressing, locking, latency, consistency, and update behavior.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect prototypes and tests the redesigned access path, migration, dual-read or cutover, and recovery behavior.
Details.errorCorrection: Scalability alone does not preserve correctness, uncontrolled dual writes diverge, and S3 is not a transparent block device.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Object redesign can improve scale but requires application and data-model work.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A storage model mismatch can create correctness and latency failure.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Dual writes require explicit consistency and reconciliation controls.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Object storage needs an application-compatible access model or adapter.
